mainTopic: Switching the names of רבי מאיר and רבי יוסי on a נדר 'until before פסח,' then a new משנה on how long נדרים tied to harvests and summer last.
overview: The amud opens by finishing the גמרא's explanation of the argument about a נדר 'until before פסח': רבי מאיר holds a person does not put himself into doubt, and רבי יוסי holds he does. A משנה from קידושין about a father who betrothed 'my older daughter' seems to say the opposite, since there רבי מאיר is strict and רבי יוסי is lenient. רב answers that the names in our משנה must be switched, and a ברייתא backs this up. Then a new משנה teaches that a נדר 'until the harvest' lasts only until the harvest begins. It gives a rule: for a fixed date, 'until it arrives' means until it starts and 'until it will be' means until it ends, while for a time that is not fixed both mean until it starts. It also defines 'summer' as starting when people bring in fruit in baskets and ending when they put away their fig knives. The גמרא explains that the baskets are fig baskets, brings an argument over whether grapes count as 'summer fruit,' and teaches that summer ends once most people have put their knives away.

steps.title: Explaining the argument as a dispute about putting oneself in doubt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its explanation of the argument in our משנה: רבי מאיר holds a person does not put himself into a doubtful situation, and רבי יוסי holds that he does.
steps.simpleTranslation: [Is it that רבי מאיר holds a person does not put himself] into doubt, and רבי יוסי holds a person does put himself into doubt?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is offering a way to understand the argument between רבי מאיר and רבי יוסי about a vow 'until before פסח.' It is also setting up the contradiction that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On this reading, רבי מאיר takes the short, certain meaning of the vow, so it ends when פסח arrives. רבי יוסי says a person is willing to forbid himself even during the doubtful time, so the vow lasts longer. So רבי מאיר comes out lenient here and רבי יוסי comes out strict.

keyTerms.meaning: A person puts himself into a situation of doubt (he accepts the stricter, doubtful meaning of his own words)

phrases.english: into doubt, and Rabbi Yosei holds:
phrases.notes: The question began just before this line: 'Is it that רבי מאיר holds a person does not put himself' into doubt?

phrases.english: a person does put himself into doubt?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי סָבַר: מְעַיֵּיל אִינִישׁ נַפְשֵׁיהּ לִסְפֵיקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the גמרא's question about the משנה, which started on the previous section of the daf.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the argument in the משנה about whether a person puts himself into a doubtful situation, with רבי מאיר saying no and רבי יוסי saying yes?

steps.title: A contradiction from the case of the betrothed older daughter: רבי מאיר's view
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה from קידושין. A father with two sets of daughters says he betrothed 'my older daughter' and doesn't know which one he meant. רבי מאיר forbids every daughter who could be called 'older.'
steps.simpleTranslation: They contradicted this: Someone has two groups of daughters from two wives. He said, 'I betrothed my older daughter, and I do not know if it was the oldest of the older group, the oldest of the younger group, or the younger of the older group, who is older than the oldest of the younger group.' All of them are forbidden, says רבי מאיר, except the youngest of the younger group.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the explanation it just gave. It quotes a case where רבי מאיר is strict and worries about every possible meaning of 'my older daughter.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each of three daughters could be called 'the older one' in some sense, and רבי מאיר forbids all three to marry anyone else. That means רבי מאיר does take the doubtful meanings seriously. It sounds like he holds a person does put himself into doubt, which is the opposite of what step 1 said.

keyTerms.meaning: And they contradicted it (the גמרא sets one source against another)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two cases. Our משנה is about a vow 'until before פסח.' This משנה is about betrothing a daughter. The גמרא is only comparing how strict each תנא is when words are unclear.

phrases.english: And they contradicted it:

phrases.aramaic: מִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ שְׁתֵּי כִּיתֵּי בָנוֹת
phrases.english: One who has two groups of daughters
from two wives,
and he said: I betrothed my older daughter,
and I do not know if it was the older of the older group,
or the older of the younger group,
or the younger of the older group,
who is older than the older of the younger group —
all of them are forbidden; these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
Except for the younger of the younger group.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 1's picture of רבי מאיר as the lenient one.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי מאיר holds a person does not put himself into doubt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In קידושין, רבי מאיר forbids every daughter who might be meant, so he does take the doubtful meanings into account, the opposite of step 1.

steps.title: The same case: רבי יוסי's lenient view
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי permits all the daughters except the oldest of the older group, meaning he takes only the most obvious meaning of 'older daughter.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says: All of them are permitted, except the oldest of the older group.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting the משנה. This completes the contradiction, because רבי יוסי turns out to be the lenient one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי says that by 'my older daughter' the father meant only the plain, clearest meaning, the oldest daughter overall. So here רבי יוסי does not take the doubtful meanings into account, which is the opposite of step 1, where he was the strict one. Both תנאים now seem flipped compared to our משנה.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says: All of them are permitted,
except for the older of the older group.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the quote begun in step 2 and finishes the contradiction.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי יוסי holds a person does put himself into doubt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In קידושין, רבי יוסי takes only the narrowest meaning of the words, so he does not take the doubt into account.

steps.title: רב: switch the names in our משנה
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא בר אבדימי quotes רב: the opinions in our משנה are reversed. רבי מאיר is really the strict one, and רבי יוסי is the lenient one.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא בר אבדימי said in the name of רב: The opinions are switched.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction. It does not reinterpret anything; it simply swaps the names in our משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the names are swapped, רבי מאיר is strict in both places and takes the doubtful meaning into account, and רבי יוסי is lenient in both places. So the two תנאים stay consistent across both משניות.

keyTerms.meaning: The opinions are switched (the names attached to each view must be reversed)

steps.confusionAlert: Only our משנה in נדרים gets switched. The משנה in קידושין stays the way it is written.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בַּר אַבְדִּימִי אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Avdimi said that Rav said:
The opinions are switched.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in steps 2 and 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reversing which name goes with which view in our משנה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought רבי מאיר was lenient and רבי יוסי strict on the vow 'until before פסח.'
steps.terutzMaskana: The names are switched, so רבי מאיר is strict and רבי יוסי lenient, matching קידושין.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the גמרא prefers to keep each תנא consistent, even if that means reversing the names in a משנה.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports the switch
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא gives a general rule: for any vow 'until before' a fixed time, רבי מאיר says the vow lasts until that time ends, and רבי יוסי says only until it arrives, which is the switched version.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it was taught in a ברייתא: This is the rule. For anything with a fixed time, if someone said 'until before' it, רבי מאיר says the vow lasts until the time ends, and רבי יוסי says until it arrives.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא as proof that רב was right to switch the names.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this ברייתא, רבי מאיר holds the vow lasts longer, through the whole fixed time, so he is the strict one. רבי יוסי ends it as soon as the time arrives, so he is the lenient one. This matches רב's switched version and the משנה in קידושין.

keyTerms.meaning: Its time is fixed (an event on a set date)
Until it goes out (until the time ends)
Until it arrives (until the time begins)

steps.whatToRemember: After the switch: on a vow 'until before' a fixed time, רבי מאיר is strict (until it ends) and רבי יוסי is lenient (until it arrives). This fits how they rule on the 'older daughter' case in קידושין.

phrases.english: And it was taught: This is the rule:
Anything whose time is fixed,
and he said 'until before' it —
phrases.notes: He means a vow like 'no wine for me until before פסח.'

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says: until it ends,
and Rabbi Yosei says: until it arrives.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב's answer in step 4 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רב's claim that the names in our משנה are switched.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא stating the general rule for vows 'until before' a fixed time, with רבי מאיר strict and רבי יוסי lenient.

steps.title: A vow until the harvest lasts only until the harvest begins
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a נדר 'until the grain, grape, or olive harvest' lasts only until that harvest arrives.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone vows 'until the grain harvest,' 'until the grape harvest,' or 'until the olive harvest,' the item is forbidden to him only until that harvest arrives.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It says that a נדר tied to a harvest lasts only until the harvest starts, not until it is over.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The person named a season, so we need to know whether the נדר ends when the season starts or when it finishes. The משנה says it ends when the season starts. The next line gives the rule behind this ruling.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
"Until the grain harvest," "until the grape harvest,"
"until the olive harvest" —
it is forbidden only until it arrives.
phrases.notes: He means the item is forbidden only until the harvest season begins.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ עַד הַקָּצִיר עַד הַבָּצִיר עַד הַמָּסִיק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה after the previous discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A נדר until a harvest lasts only until the harvest begins.

steps.title: The rule for fixed and unfixed times
steps.stepSummary: The משנה gives the rule. For a fixed date, the wording decides whether the נדר ends at the start or the end. For an unfixed time, it always ends at the start.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is the rule. If the occasion has a fixed date and he said 'until it arrives,' the item is forbidden until it arrives. If he said 'until it will be,' it is forbidden until the occasion is over. If the occasion has no fixed date, then whether he said 'until it will be' or 'until it arrives,' it is forbidden only until it arrives.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a general rule that explains its ruling about the harvests.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a fixed date, the person could have simply said 'until it arrives.' So when he says 'until it will be,' he must mean 'until it is over.' With a time that is not fixed, both wordings mean only until it begins. Harvests have no exact date, so they fall into the second group, which is why step 6 said 'only until it arrives.'

keyTerms.meaning: Its time is fixed (it falls on a set date)
Until it goes out (until it ends)

steps.confusionAlert: 'Until it will be' sounds like it means the same as 'until it arrives.' For a fixed date, though, it means until the occasion is over.
steps.whyThisMatters: This rule decides how long many seasonal נדרים last, and it shows how the wording of a נדר changes its meaning.

phrases.english: This is the rule:
anything whose time is fixed,
and he said: "Until it arrives" —
it is forbidden until it arrives.
If he said: "Until it will be" —
it is forbidden until it goes out.
phrases.notes: 'Goes out' here means the occasion is completely over.

phrases.english: And anything whose time is not fixed,
whether he said "Until it will be,"
or he said "Until it arrives" —
it is forbidden only until it arrives.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the general rule behind the harvest ruling in step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For a fixed time, 'until it arrives' means until it starts and 'until it will be' means until it ends. For an unfixed time, both mean until it starts.

steps.title: How long a vow until summer lasts
steps.stepSummary: The משנה defines 'summer' by the fig season. It begins when people bring figs home in baskets and ends when they put away the fig knives.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said 'until the summer' or 'until it will be summer,' the נדר lasts until people begin bringing fruit home in baskets. If he said 'until the summer passes,' it lasts until people fold up and put away their cutting knives.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה explains when 'summer' starts and when it ends, for someone who made his נדר depend on it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here 'summer' is a farming season, not a calendar date. It is not fixed, so 'until it will be summer' also means only until summer starts. Saying 'until it passes' clearly means until it is over, which is when the cutting work stops.

keyTerms.meaning: Summer, the season of gathering (and cutting) figs

phrases.english: "Until the summer,"
"until it will be summer" —
until the people begin
to bring in [fruit] in baskets.
"Until the summer passes" —
until they fold up the knives.
phrases.notes: These are the knives used for cutting figs. Once they are put away, the season is over.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the time rules to the specific word 'summer.'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Summer begins when people bring fruit home in baskets and ends when they put away the cutting knives.

steps.title: The baskets in the משנה hold figs, not grapes
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a teaching that the 'basket' in the משנה means a basket of figs.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: the 'basket' the משנה spoke about is a basket of figs, not a basket of grapes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by explaining one word in the משנה: whose baskets mark the start of summer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This tells us summer starts when figs are brought in. It does not depend on when grapes are brought in, so the start of summer is tied to the fig harvest.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
It was taught:
The "basket" that they spoke of —
is a basket of figs,
and not a basket of grapes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the word 'baskets' from the end of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The baskets that mark the start of summer are fig baskets.

steps.title: An argument over whether grapes count as summer fruit
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that a נדר from 'summer fruit' forbids only figs. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says grapes are included too.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: someone who vows not to eat 'summer fruit' is forbidden only figs. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says grapes are included along with figs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a related ברייתא that also connects the word 'summer' to figs. It records an argument about grapes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תנא קמא agrees with the teaching in step 9 that 'summer' means figs only. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל widens 'summer fruit' to include grapes. The גמרא will next ask for the reason behind each view.

phrases.english: It was taught in a ברייתא:
One who vows against summer fruit —
is forbidden only in figs.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
Grapes are included with figs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that links 'summer' to figs, like step 9, and adds an argument about grapes.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תנא קמא: 'summer fruit' means figs only. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: grapes are included too.

steps.title: Why does the first opinion limit summer fruit to figs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reasoning of תנא קמא.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of תנא קמא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why תנא קמא counts only figs as 'summer fruit.' This sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gave rulings without reasons. The גמרא wants to know what makes figs, and not grapes, 'summer fruit' for תנא קמא.

phrases.english: What is the reason of the first tanna?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the first view in the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why תנא קמא counts only figs as summer fruit.

steps.title: Figs are cut by hand, and the question is whether ripe grapes are too
steps.stepSummary: תנא קמא holds that only figs are cut off by hand. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that very ripe grapes are also cut off by hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: He holds that figs are cut off by hand, but grapes are not cut off by hand. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that grapes too, when they are fully ripe, are cut off by hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that both sides agree 'summer fruit' means fruit picked by hand. They argue only about whether grapes are picked that way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word for 'cut off' (מִיקַּצְצָן) sounds like קַיִץ, so 'summer fruit' is fruit that is cut off by hand. תנא קמא says grapes need a tool, so they are left out. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says fully ripe grapes come off by hand, so they are included.
steps.whatToRemember: Both opinions define 'summer fruit' as fruit picked by hand. They argue only about whether ripe grapes are picked by hand.

phrases.english: He holds:
figs are cut off by hand,
phrases.notes: מיקצצן sounds like קיץ. That is why being cut by hand decides what counts as 'summer fruit.'

phrases.english: grapes are not cut off by hand.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds:
grapes too, when they are fully ripe —
are cut off by hand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 11 and explains the other opinion as well.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Summer fruit is fruit cut off by hand. תנא קמא says grapes are not cut by hand. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says fully ripe grapes are.

steps.title: Summer ends when most people put away their fig knives
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's phrase 'until the summer has passed,' which means until the fig knives are put away. A ברייתא explains that it is enough for MOST people to put their knives away.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'Until the summer has passed' means until the fig knives are put away. A ברייתא taught: until most of the knives are put away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings back the second half of the משנה, about when summer ENDS. It then quotes a ברייתא that makes the rule more exact.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's wording could sound like summer lasts until every single person has put away his fig knife. The ברייתא says no. Once most people have put their knives away, summer is over, even if a few people are still cutting figs. So the end of the נדר follows the majority.

keyTerms.meaning: Until the summer passes. This is the wording of the נדר being defined.
The special knives used to cut figs for drying.
Literally 'folded.' Here it means the knives are folded up and put away.

steps.whatToRemember: The fig season, and so 'summer' in a נדר, ends once MOST people have put away their fig knives. A few late people do not keep summer going.

phrases.english: "Until the summer has passed,"
means until the fig knives are folded up and put away.
It was taught: until MOST of the knives are folded up and put away.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back from the ברייתא about summer fruit (Steps 10-12) to the משנה's definition from Step 8, now clarifying when summer ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Summer, for a נדר, ends when the majority of people have put away their fig knives. Not every person needs to have done so.
